vignette: John, a 49-year-old married architect, witnessed a traumatic incident at his workplace three months ago that has profoundly impacted his life. The event occurred during a construction project where he was overseeing the demolition of an old building. As he was walking through one of the rooms to check on the progress, he heard loud noises and screams from behind him. He turned around just in time to see a massive section of the wall collapse, burying several workers underneath the debris. Since that day, John has been plagued by intense feelings of vulnerability and helplessness. The memories of the event have become fragmented and confusing; he cannot put them in the right sequence or find words to describe what exactly happened. This confusion leads him to experience vivid flashbacks where it feels as though the wall is collapsing again, bringing with it a sense of nausea that makes his stomach churn. The specific triggers from this traumatic event are deeply rooted in his daily life. Whenever he encounters violence-be it on TV or hearing about it in the news-he relives those moments of helplessness and fear. The smell of dust and debris can transport him back to that day, making it hard for him to stay focused at work. John has developed a strong need to feel safe by having his back against a wall where he can see everything around him. This behavior is particularly evident in his architectural firm, where he often finds himself seeking out positions near walls or entrances during meetings. He frequently scans exits as soon as he enters any room or building, which sometimes makes colleagues and clients question his level of engagement. The incident has also isolated John from others. He feels set apart and disconnected, believing that there is something inherently wrong with him that made this event happen to him and those around him. This deep-seated belief in intrinsic fault fuels a profound sense of helplessness, leading him to feel as though he cannot prevent bad things from happening again. John's wife has noticed significant changes in his behavior over the past few months. He avoids going out and often makes excuses to stay home, which has strained their relationship. His work performance has also suffered; colleagues have reported that John seems distracted and less engaged than before, leading to missed deadlines and a general decline in productivity. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly distressing flashback while he was at a social event with his wife. The sound of laughter combined with the smell of food triggered intense nausea and a sudden urge to flee the room. He felt jumpy and easily startled, and it became clear that these episodes were not only affecting him but also causing concern for those around him. John is now seeking psychological help because he hopes to regain control over his life. What frightens him most is the possibility of being trapped in a cycle where he cannot protect himself or those he loves from harm again. He hopes therapy will provide strategies to cope with his symptoms and reconnect with others, allowing him to return to a state of normalcy and security.
